concepts.heading: Historical & Colonial Roots of Relationship Norms
concepts.alt: A guide unrolling a long old scroll that turns into a winding road
concepts.plain: Our ideas about love and marriage come from a particular time and place.

concepts.heading: A Brief History of "Normal"
concepts.alt: Each standing in a differently shaped little house, four houses side by side
concepts.plain: Before colonial rule, people around the world lived and loved in many different ways.

concepts.heading: How "Love" Became Mandatory
concepts.alt: A guide holding a calendar page and a heart, looking surprised
concepts.plain: Marrying for love is only about 250 years old.

concepts.heading: The Colonial Project of "Proper" Relationships
concepts.plain: Colonizers forced one model on people: one man, one woman, the man in charge.

concepts.heading: The Ongoing Impact
concepts.alt: A guide holding a thick old rulebook with a padlock on it
concepts.plain: Those rules still live on in laws, religion and what people expect.

concepts.heading: Intersections with Race
concepts.plain: For Black Americans, slavery tore families apart, and that harm still echoes.

checks.prompt: How old is the idea of marrying mainly for love?
checks.explanation: About 250 years. Historian Stephanie Coontz documents in Marriage, a History that romantic love as the basis for marriage is only about 250 years old.

checks.prompt: Where do colonial relationship norms still show up today?
checks.explanation: In legal systems. Colonial norms persist through legal systems that only recognize certain kinds of partnership.

01becfdf-4e05-438a-be92-e53c7deae335.takeaway: Many relationship "rules" are recent and local, not natural laws.

concepts.heading: Dismantling Heteronormativity & Amatonormativity
concepts.alt: A guide pulling back a stage curtain to reveal turning gears behind it
concepts.plain: Hidden assumptions shape what we think a relationship should be.

concepts.heading: What Is Heteronormativity?
concepts.alt: A guide standing at a fork where one path is paved and the others are grassy trails
concepts.plain: Heteronormativity is the belief that being straight is the normal default.

concepts.heading: What Is Amatonormativity?
concepts.alt: A in the middle hugging her two best friends, all laughing
concepts.plain: Amatonormativity is the belief that everyone needs one romantic partner to be complete.

concepts.heading: The Intersection with Race, Class, and Disability
concepts.plain: These pressures hit harder depending on your race, money and ability.

concepts.heading: Practical Dismantling
concepts.alt: A guide crossing items off a long checklist and tossing it over his shoulder
concepts.plain: Start by noticing your own words and choices, then pick what you actually want.

options: Straight relationships are the default and best
checks.explanation: Straight relationships are the default and best. Heteronormativity is the assumption that heterosexual relationships are the default, natural, and superior form of human bonding.

Pursue one central romantic relationship. Coined by philosopher Elizabeth Brake, amatonormativity is the assumption that everyone should pursue a central, exclusive romantic relationship as their primary source of love and life partnership.

42675418-3f53-4fe2-a0f4-4ff2792c1cdd.takeaway: You do not have to follow the default script of one straight, romantic couple.

concepts.heading: Cultural Diversity in Love & Family
concepts.alt: Four guides standing around a globe, each pointing at a different place
concepts.plain: Around the world, people have organised love and family in very different ways.

concepts.heading: Relationship Structures Across Cultures
concepts.alt: A guide holding a world map with little houses of different shapes pinned on it
concepts.plain: Some cultures have had one wife with several husbands, shared child-raising and more.

concepts.heading: What Western Culture Can Learn
concepts.alt: A guide having a lightbulb moment while reading a book
concepts.plain: There is more than one workable way to build a family.

concepts.heading: The Danger of Romanticizing
concepts.alt: A guide admiring a museum display case from a respectful distance, hands behind her back
concepts.plain: Learn from other cultures without copying them or making them sound perfect.

concepts.heading: Modern Applications
concepts.alt: A guide sketching a house plan at a drafting table
concepts.plain: Use these ideas to think about what you want in your own relationships.

checks.prompt: Polyandry, practised historically in Tibet and Nepal, means…
options: One woman married to several men
One man married to several women
checks.explanation: One woman married to several men. In Tibet and Nepal, women historically married multiple brothers, which kept family land together.

checks.prompt: What should you avoid when learning from other cultures?
checks.explanation: Romanticizing or appropriating them. While learning from diverse cultures is valuable, it's important to avoid romanticizing or appropriating.

897440b3-98e0-4190-9ee1-bb43474c0344.takeaway: People have built love and family in many ways. Learn from them with respect.

concepts.heading: Building Your Own Relationship Framework
concepts.alt: At a drafting table drawing a heart-shaped blueprint
concepts.plain: Now you can design relationships that actually fit you.

concepts.heading: The Relationship Design Process
concepts.alt: A guide walking along a circular path of arrows, holding a notebook
concepts.plain: Building your own approach is ongoing. Try, check, adjust.

concepts.heading: Tools for Framework Building
concepts.alt: Two guides sharing a large menu card decorated with hearts, choosing together
concepts.plain: Think of relationships as a menu to choose from, not an escalator with one direction.

concepts.heading: Common Pitfalls
concepts.alt: A guide stumbling lightly over a pile of rule books
concepts.plain: Common traps: only rebelling, making too many rules, or copying someone else.

concepts.heading: Living Your Framework
concepts.alt: A guide watering a small potted plant with heart-shaped leaves
concepts.plain: Real life will test your plan. Update it as you learn.

options: An escalator with a single path upward
checks.explanation: An escalator with a single path upward. The Relationship Menu: Rather than an escalator (a single path upward), think of relationships as a menu.

options: Building your framework only in opposition to the mainstream
checks.explanation: Building your framework only in opposition to the mainstream. It means building your framework purely against mainstream culture rather than toward what you genuinely want.

51c04283-5c81-49e6-b053-a76659acacd7.takeaway: Design your relationships on purpose, around what you truly want, and keep adjusting.
